transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Martin Reyes (Aurum CTO), Sofia Lang (Aurum Head of ML), Derek Holt (Infra Manager), Nina Park (Procurement)

Summary: Discovery focused on Dedicated capacity requirements: isolation, reserved GPU sizing, burst/burstback strategy, scaling expectations, security controls (SOC2, KMS), and pilot/benchmark next steps. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; leaning Dedicated for data isolation and predictable latency/cost.

Topics: dedicated capacity sizing, isolation & network (VPC), burst policies, autoscaling, monitoring, runbook, procurement timeline, security/compliance, pilot timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, for the Aurum call. Alex from Redwood here, with Priya. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Martin Reyes: Good, thanks. Busy week but yeah we're ready.
[00:11] Sofia Lang: Hi all.
[00:12] Derek Holt: Afternoon.
[00:13] Nina Park: Hi, thanks.
[00:15] Alex Chen: Awesome. Quick agenda - we'll do context/requirements, dig into dedicated capacity and isolation needs, discuss burst and scaling expectations, and then capture next steps. Priya will jump into some technical clarifying questions. Sound good?
[00:27] Martin Reyes: Sounds good. We're trying to confirm whether dedicated reserved GPUs is the right path for us vs just using hosted endpoints. The main driver is regulatory and customer data isolation - we can't have multi-tenant data residency for certain workloads.
[00:41] Priya Patel: Got it. When you say isolation, is the requirement network level isolation (VPC), phys isolation, or both? Also are you thinking on-prem or cloud VPC private deployment?
[00:53] Sofia Lang: For now it's cloud VPC, but we do need complete tenancy isolation - no shared instances with other customers. Physically dedicated GPUs are preferred for the highest risk models, especially PII-related pipelines.
[01:07] Derek Holt: To add, we have a mix - most inference is non-PII but about 20% of requests hit the regulated flow where data must never leave our control. We want a configuration where the dedicated cluster serves those flows, with burst capacity for peak times.
[01:21] Alex Chen: Perfect. That's exactly the use case Redwood Dedicated was designed for - reserved GPU pools in your VPC with customer-managed networking and KMS integration. Let me ask a few baseline questions on QPS and latency expectations.
[01:33] Priya Patel: Yeah, what are your typical RPS and percentiles? Also model sizes - are you running Llama-like 7B/13B or larger 70B+?
[01:42] Sofia Lang: Our baseline is about 50 RPS on the regulated path, peaks up to 250 RPS for end-of-day batch processing windows. Models are mixed: primarily 13B and a few 70B runs for higher fidelity tasks. Latency target is 150ms p95 for the regulated path, we'd accept slightly higher for big 70B runs but prefer below 500ms.
[02:02] Priya Patel: Okay that helps. For 13B models we can hit 150ms p95 on an A100-class setup with proper batching disabled for low latency; for 70B we typically recommend model sharding and larger instance shapes which pushes tail latency up. Are you okay with per-model SLOs and fallbacks to smaller variants during peak?
[02:18] Martin Reyes: Potentially. We need deterministic worst-case SLAs though - customers require contractual guarantees. Can you commit to tail latency SLOs on Dedicated?
[02:26] Alex Chen: We offer latency targets backed in Dedicated SLAs; specifics depend on committed capacity and model shape. Typically a reserved pool with autoscaling policies and burst buffers can keep p95 under target. We also support automatic fallback to quantized variants or smaller models during capacity constraints.
[02:42] Derek Holt: How does burst work exactly? We have big spikes for reporting windows and can't afford failures.
[02:48] Priya Patel: Burst is handled two ways - short term burst using burst capacity within your Dedicated pool (reserved but idle instances that can be assigned quickly), and cross-region fallback to our hosted pool if you allow it. Since you said you want strict isolation, cross-tenant fallback might be a no. There's also an option to provision a cold standby that we can spin up, but that has longer warm-up time.
[03:09] Nina Park: We can't use cross-tenant fallback for regulated flows. What is warm-up time for cold standby?
[03:14] Priya Patel: Cold standby typically 8-20 minutes to fully initialize model KV caches for large models - depends on weights and compilation. Warm standby where we keep kernels and weights resident reduces warm-up to under 2 minutes but costs more.
[03:28] Sofia Lang: That 8-20 minutes is a concern. Our spike windows are sometimes unpredictable. Do you support preemptible burst instances or autoscale faster?
[03:36] Alex Chen: We can do configurable autoscale policies with aggressive policies for the regulated route - e.g. keep a minimum hot pool, plus a burst buffer. You can also configure sequence-length aware batching that helps throughput without hurting p95 as long as you cap batch sizes. There are cost trade-offs.
[03:53] Martin Reyes: Let's talk numbers - what's a reasonable reserved pool for 50 RPS baseline for 13B and ability to spike to 250? Also cost ballpark.
[04:03] Priya Patel: Very rough: for low-latency 13B you might want 2-3 A100 GPUs active for 50 RPS depending on concurrency and sequence length. For headroom to 250, add burst capacity of 6-8 GPUs or scale to 8 GPUs total. For 70B, each request might need model parallelism across multiple GPUs. We'll produce an exact sizing after we see traces. Cost depends on region and commit term; we'll include committed-discount pricing in the follow-up.
[04:28] Derek Holt: Ok please include commit tiers. Also curious about tooling - monitoring, tracing, token-level cost, and per-route dashboards.
[04:36] Alex Chen: Redwood Console gives per-route latency and token breakdowns, KV cache hit rates, and tracing hooks. You can create per-route policies, rollouts, and automatic rollback. We also surface per-token unit costs so you can tune prompt templates.
[04:50] Sofia Lang: About KV caching - does the runtime persist KV cache across restarts, or is it in-memory? We need to avoid cold cache penalties.
[04:58] Priya Patel: The KV cache is in-memory in the serving nodes; we support warm standby nodes that keep KV persistent. For stateful workloads we also have prefix caching and sticky routing to improve cache locality. Sometimes the transcripts of our infra docs say "k v cache" in different ways, so sorry if I mis-say it.
[05:14] Martin Reyes: No worries. Security: SOC2, ISO, encryption, KMS - we need customer-managed keys and audit logs. Also SSO and RBAC.
[05:23] Alex Chen: Understood. Dedicated supports KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs shipped to your SIEM, SAML SSO, and fine-grained RBAC. We'll share SOC2/ISO attestation and a security architecture doc after this call.
[05:33] Nina Park: Procurement: what's the typical term and cancellation? We need clarity for PO.
[05:38] Alex Chen: Standard is monthly or annual committed capacity contracts for Dedicated. There's also a pilot agreement for short proofs-of-concept. We'll send the contract templates.
[05:46] Derek Holt: On data residency - logs and metrics, are they stored in our VPC or do some telemetry go back to Redwood?
[05:52] Priya Patel: For Private and Dedicated in-VPC deployments, telemetry can be routed to your logging endpoints. We do offer optional metrics streaming to Redwood for managed observability, but for regulated customers we can restrict that and keep logs within your control.
[06:06] Sofia Lang: Ok great. Let's dive into the pilot/benchmark. We want to run our 13B model and a sampled 70B workload. Expectations: get latency p95 and cost per 1k tokens.
[06:18] Priya Patel: For the benchmark we typically need: model artifact access (or a compatible buildpack), sample request traces (RPS timeline, sequence length distribution), target SLOs, and some test dataset. We'll provision a small dedicated pool for a 2-week pilot to run repeatable tests.
[06:33] Martin Reyes: Who owns model artifacts? We prefer to bring our own models. Is that supported?
[06:37] Alex Chen: Yes BYO models are supported; we can also host curated models. For BYO we need the model in a compatible format and we'll provide onboarding docs and a model verification run.
[06:46] Nina Park: About invoices - will we be billed for the standby GPUs even if not used?
[06:50] Alex Chen: For reserved capacity, you pay for committed capacity. There's a tiered structure: committed (lower unit cost) plus overage/burst fees if you exceed committed baseline. Warm standby options are priced separately. We'll include pricing scenarios.
[07:03] Derek Holt: Network egress - any hidden egress costs?
[07:07] Priya Patel: Egress is typical cloud egress; if Dedicated is in your VPC you mostly control egress routing and costs. We'll call out any Redwood-managed control plane egress in the sec doc.
[07:18] Martin Reyes: Any customer references that did similar regulated deployments?
[07:21] Alex Chen: Yes - we have a banking customer and a healthcare provider on Dedicated; we can provide redacted reference material. I'll include that.
[07:29] Sofia Lang: Ok, Priya - on the infrastructure side, what's the recommended autoscale policy to keep p95 sub-150ms for 13B while minimizing cost?
[07:38] Priya Patel: Recommend minimum hot pool to cover baseline RPS (2 GPUs), a buffer of 2 GPUs in warm standby, and aggressive scale-up policy triggered by 75% GPU utilization on average plus request queue thresholds. Also set per-route limits so regulated flows have priority scheduling and don't get queued behind non-regulated.
[07:56] Derek Holt: How do you prioritize? We need guaranteed isolation of regulated route so no noisy neighbor interference.
[08:02] Priya Patel: You can create per-route resource pools with guaranteed reservations. Regulated route assigned to its own reserved pool - no other tenants run there. For burst you can allow it to draw from a dedicated burst buffer only. That meets isolation requirements.
[08:16] Martin Reyes: Migration concerns - what's the effort to onboard?
[08:20] Alex Chen: Typical onboarding is 2-6 weeks: contract, infra setup, VPC peering, KMS integration, model onboarding, and run benchmark. For BYO models that'll add time if there's custom compilation. Priya will help scope technical effort.
[08:33] Priya Patel: On the compilation point, large models sometimes need optimized kernels; if you use quantized variants that reduces memory and improves throughput but may change output quality slightly. We'll recommend quantization profiles after we see evaluation traces.
[08:47] Sofia Lang: Output quality is a factor; we can't accept regressions. How do you guard against quality shifts when using quantization or model fallback?
[08:55] Alex Chen: We have Redwood Optimize suggestions and quality monitoring that ties to prompt/eval sets - if a regression is detected we raise an alert and can automatically rollback. We'll also run A/B tests during rollout.
[09:07] Nina Park: Procurement timeline - we're aiming to select vendor by end of month and kickoff pilot mid-next month. Is that feasible?
[09:13] Alex Chen: Yes that's feasible. We'll prioritize getting you a pricing deck and security package this week.
[09:18] Martin Reyes: Great. Technical detail - Priya, what telemetry do you need from us for sizing?
[09:23] Priya Patel: Sample traces with timestamped request size, sequence lengths, tokens per request, concurrency, and model id. Also any percentiles you currently capture. If you can share a day of traffic and a peak day, that'd be ideal.
[09:35] Derek Holt: We'll extract those and share. Also include any sample prompts and expected max sequence length.
[09:40] Alex Chen: Perfect. Any other concerns?
[09:42] Sofia Lang: One more on SLA credits - if latency SLOs fail, what's the typical credit?
[09:47] Alex Chen: We have standard SLA credit policies based on severity and uptime; for Dedicated we can negotiate tighter terms with higher credits as part of the committed contract. We'll include examples.
[09:58] Martin Reyes: Competitors - we're also talking to MegaCloud AI and OnPremia. They pitched fixed pricing and hardware-lifecycle control. Curious on Redwood's angle.
[10:08] Alex Chen: Our differentiator is production-first runtime with unified ops across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, and tooling to manage unit economics: RBAC, cost per token, and quality monitors integrated.
[10:18] Nina Park: Ok noted.
[10:20] Priya Patel: Quick note - for your 70B runs we recommend testing sharded execution vs dist inference to measure latency; we can provide both patterns in the benchmark.
[10:29] Sofia Lang: Sounds good.
[10:31] Alex Chen: Alright let's recap next steps - we'll send pricing and contract templates, SOC2/ISO and KMS integration notes, a benchmark plan, and schedule the 90-minute benchmark session next week. Derek will send traces and sample prompts. Nina will share procurement timeline.
[10:48] Martin Reyes: That works.
[10:50] Derek Holt: I'll get the traces out today or tomorrow.
[10:53] Nina Park: We'll confirm PO process and timeline by 3/10.
[10:56] Alex Chen: Great, thanks everyone. Priya and I will follow up.
[10:59] Sofia Lang: Thanks all.
[11:00] Alex Chen: End meeting.

Notes about transcription: occasional terms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., "k v cache" vs "KV cache"), some proper nouns simplified.
